concepts.name: Definition and Core Mechanism of Demand-Pull Inflation
key_dimensions: Classical definition: 'Too much money chasing too few goods'
Distinction from cost-push inflation — demand-side vs supply-side origin
Role of aggregate demand (AD) exceeding aggregate supply (AS) at full employment
UPSC trap: Demand-pull can co-exist with cost-push (stagflation vs. pure demand-pull)

concepts.name: Keynesian vs. Monetarist Explanations of Demand-Pull Inflation
key_dimensions: Keynesian view: Excess aggregate expenditure (C+I+G+NX) beyond full-employment output causes inflationary gap
Monetarist view (Milton Friedman): 'Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon' — excess money supply drives demand
Policy implication difference: Keynesians favor fiscal contraction; Monetarists favor money supply control
UPSC trap: Distinguishing which school supports which anti-inflation tool

concepts.name: Inflationary Gap Concept
key_dimensions: Definition: Difference between actual aggregate demand and the level of AD consistent with full employment output
Graphical representation on AD-AS framework — rightward shift of AD beyond potential GDP
Distinction from output gap (negative vs. positive output gap)
UPSC trap: Inflationary gap ≠ inflation rate; it is the excess demand that causes inflation

concepts.name: Role of Government Expenditure (Fiscal Policy) in Triggering Demand-Pull Inflation
key_dimensions: Expansionary fiscal policy (increased G or tax cuts) raises aggregate demand
Deficit financing and monetization of fiscal deficit as a direct inflationary channel
FRBM Act, 2003 — fiscal consolidation as an anti-inflationary framework in India
UPSC trap: Revenue deficit is more inflationary than capital deficit — consumption vs. investment spending

concepts.name: Monetary Expansion and Credit Growth as Drivers of Demand-Pull Inflation
key_dimensions: Excess money supply (M3 growth) increasing purchasing power and aggregate demand
Role of RBI's monetary policy tools (Repo rate, CRR, SLR) in controlling credit-driven demand
Quantitative easing in advanced economies and imported demand-pull inflation via capital flows
UPSC trap: CRR reduction increases money multiplier — indirect but powerful demand stimulator

concepts.name: Consumer Confidence and Private Consumption as Demand-Pull Triggers
key_dimensions: Wealth effect: Rising asset prices (stocks, real estate) boosting consumer spending
Permanent Income Hypothesis (Friedman) — expectations of future income driving current consumption
Post-pandemic pent-up demand as a real-world example of sudden demand surge
UPSC trap: High consumer confidence can cause demand-pull even without monetary expansion

concepts.name: Investment Boom and Its Contribution to Demand-Pull Inflation
key_dimensions: Surge in private investment increases demand for capital goods, labor, and raw materials
Accelerator principle: Rising consumption demand amplifying investment demand
Short-run vs. long-run effect — investment adds to demand now but increases supply capacity later (reducing inflation eventually)
UPSC trap: Investment-led demand-pull is self-correcting in the long run unlike consumption-led demand-pull

concepts.name: Export Boom and External Demand as a Source of Demand-Pull Inflation
key_dimensions: Rise in foreign demand (NX component of AD) pulling domestic prices upward
Currency depreciation making exports cheaper, boosting foreign demand but raising domestic prices
India-specific: Commodity export booms (agricultural, IT services surge) and domestic price implications
UPSC trap: Export-led demand-pull is often overlooked; candidates focus only on domestic demand sources

concepts.name: Demand-Pull Inflation and the Phillips Curve
key_dimensions: Original Phillips Curve: Inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation — demand expansion reduces unemployment but raises inflation
Short-run Phillips Curve (SRPC) vs. Long-run Phillips Curve (LRPC) — LRPC is vertical at natural rate of unemployment (NAIRU)
Stagflation of 1970s discrediting the stable Phillips Curve trade-off
UPSC trap: LRPC being vertical implies no long-run trade-off — demand-pull inflation has no permanent output benefit

concepts.name: Demand-Pull Inflation in the AD-AS Framework
key_dimensions: Rightward shift of AD curve along an upward-sloping SRAS — both price level and output rise initially
Long-run adjustment: LRAS is vertical; only price level rises with no output gain
Supply-side bottlenecks amplifying demand-pull (inelastic AS steepening the curve)
UPSC trap: In the short run, demand-pull raises both output and prices — not 'only prices'

concepts.name: Sectoral Demand-Pull Inflation: Specific Markets vs. General Price Level
key_dimensions: Demand surge in specific sectors (housing, food, fuel) causing sectoral inflation vs. generalized inflation
Spillover effect: Sectoral demand-pull becoming economy-wide through wage-price spiral
India context: Food inflation driven by demand-supply mismatch in agriculture — structural demand-pull
UPSC trap: Not all sectoral price rises constitute macroeconomic demand-pull inflation

concepts.name: Demand-Pull Inflation and Wage-Price Spiral
key_dimensions: Sequence: Excess demand → price rise → workers demand higher wages → firms raise prices further
Self-reinforcing inflationary cycle — distinction from initial demand-pull trigger
Role of trade unions and collective bargaining in sustaining the spiral
UPSC trap: Wage-price spiral is a consequence/amplifier of demand-pull, not a cause — it is secondary inflation

concepts.name: Inflation Expectations and Demand-Pull Dynamics
key_dimensions: Adaptive expectations: Past inflation shapes future demand behavior (buy now before prices rise more)
Rational expectations theory: People anticipate policy and adjust — limiting effectiveness of demand stimulus
RBI's inflation targeting framework (4% ± 2%) anchoring expectations to prevent demand-pull escalation
UPSC trap: Expectation-driven demand-pull can occur even without actual monetary/fiscal expansion

concepts.name: RBI's Monetary Policy Framework as a Counter to Demand-Pull Inflation
key_dimensions: Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) framework adopted in 2016 — CPI target of 4% (±2%)
Repo rate hike → increases borrowing cost → dampens credit demand → reduces aggregate demand
MPC (Monetary Policy Committee) composition and its mandate — price stability with growth objective
UPSC trap: RBI targets CPI (retail inflation), not WPI — and its mandate is primarily demand management, not supply-side fixes

concepts.name: Demand-Pull Inflation vs. Cost-Push Inflation: Policy Response Dilemma
key_dimensions: Demand-pull: Appropriate response is contractionary monetary/fiscal policy
Cost-push: Contractionary policy worsens unemployment without fully controlling inflation (stagflation trap)
Mixed inflation (simultaneous demand-pull and cost-push): Policy dilemma of choosing between inflation and unemployment
UPSC trap: Applying demand-pull remedies to cost-push inflation is a classic policy error — frequently tested

concepts.name: Demand-Pull Inflation Measurement: WPI vs. CPI in Indian Context
key_dimensions: CPI captures demand-side consumption basket (food, housing, services) more accurately than WPI
WPI vs. CPI divergence: When WPI falls but CPI rises — indicates demand-pull in retail segments
GDP deflator as the broadest measure — reflects economy-wide demand pressure
UPSC trap: WPI declining while CPI rising is NOT contradictory — they measure different baskets at different stages

concepts.name: Demand-Pull Inflation During Economic Recovery and Business Cycles
key_dimensions: Boom phase of business cycle naturally generates demand-pull as output approaches potential GDP
Output gap turning positive (actual GDP > potential GDP) as the trigger point for demand-pull inflation
RBI's use of output gap estimation in setting monetary policy stance
UPSC trap: Demand-pull inflation signals overheating economy — it is NOT always bad (mild inflation accompanies growth)

concepts.name: Global Demand-Pull Inflation: Imported Inflation and Spillovers
key_dimensions: US Fed's quantitative easing → global liquidity surge → capital inflows into India → asset price inflation and demand stimulus
Commodity super-cycles driven by global demand (China effect) raising import costs and domestic demand simultaneously
Distinction: Imported cost-push (oil prices) vs. imported demand-pull (foreign capital fueling domestic credit boom)
UPSC trap: Not all imported inflation is cost-push — capital flow-driven asset booms create demand-pull inflation domestically

concepts.name: Demand-Pull Inflation and Income Distribution Effects
key_dimensions: Inflation as a regressive tax — fixed-income earners and poor suffer most as purchasing power erodes
Creditor-debtor redistribution: Inflation benefits borrowers (real debt burden falls) at cost of lenders
Profit inflation: Firms gain during demand-pull as prices rise faster than wages (temporarily)
UPSC trap: Demand-pull inflation initially benefits producers and borrowers — it is not uniformly harmful in the short run

concepts.name: Historical and Contemporary Case Studies of Demand-Pull Inflation
key_dimensions: Post-WWII US demand-pull: Pent-up consumer demand after wartime rationing causing price surge
India 2021-23: Post-COVID demand recovery + fiscal stimulus creating demand-pull component alongside supply-chain cost-push
Zimbabwe and Venezuela hyperinflation: Extreme demand-pull caused by uncontrolled money supply expansion
UPSC trap: India's recent inflation was MIXED (demand-pull + cost-push) — attributing it solely to demand-side is an error
